newsitem.title: USA: U.S. Gulf Coast drawing panoply of foreign crudes.
newsitem.headline: U.S. Gulf Coast drawing panoply of foreign crudes.

text.p: The U.S. Gulf Coast drew a panpoly of foreign crude offerings on Tuesday as prices continued firm, traders said.
A trading company was offering North Sea benchmark Brent was for some 50 cents under West Texas Intermediate/Cushing for around June 10-15 arrival.
A U.S. company was heard talking Brent for June 22-27 arrival, asking around WTI/Cushing minus 50-55 cents a barrel.
Traders expressed continued uncertainty about the June maintenance program in the North Sea.
"In the second half of June there are fewer alternatives (from the North Sea)," a Midwest trader said.
The June spread between WTI and Brent was around $1.70 a barrel, while dated Brent activity remained subdued amid weakening refining margins.
From Africa, Nigerian Brass River was looking for a home around June 20 for dated Brent plus $2.17 a barrel on a delivered basis, traders said.
A Saharan Blend was also on offer for June 1-5 arrival, asking around dated Brent plus $2.10 or WTI plus 25 cents a barrel.
From Asia, a European company was talking about bringing over a Vietnamese Dai Hung, a heavy sweet crude with a high pour point that normally gets swallowed up in Asia.
From Latin America, four Cusiana cargoes loading in June have been sold so far, leaving three plus one cross-month cargo.
The asking prices for the sweet grade continues to climb. A June 21-25 cargo is on offer at August WTI minus 95 cents a barrel.
Finally, a resurfacing of premiums for Exchange for Physical deals has revived talk of foreign crude deliveries into the NYMEX when the June contract expires on May 20, traders said.
EFPs were running around 12-13 cents a barrel on Tuesday.
The expiry of the May contract last month witnessed a large and unusual delivery of 2.73 million barrels of Oseberg, Brent and Bonny Light crude.

Because much of the crude was not absorbed into the market, some of it could be redelivered, prompting concerns by paper holders that they could get stuck with a crude other than WTI upon expiry, traders said.
In July, Cusiana becomes deliverable against the NYMEX crude contract, adding another foreign crude to the list of possible alternatives.
